## Experimental Design

The ACTG 320 trial [@Hammer1997] was a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial evaluating whether adding the protease inhibitor indinavir to a standard two-drug nucleoside analogue regimen improved outcomes in HIV-infected patients with CD4 cell counts of 200 cells/mm?? or fewer. A total of 1,156 adults were enrolled across multiple clinical sites. Participants were randomly assigned, in approximately equal proportions, to control (two-drug regimen plus placebo) or treatment (two-drug regimen plus indinavir). Randomization was stratified by baseline CD4 count, separately for counts below 50 cells/mm?? and counts between 51 and 200 cells/mm??. Stratified randomization was the blocking mechanism that ensured balance on the most important prognostic variable across treatment arms. The double-blind, placebo-controlled structure prevented knowledge of treatment assignment from influencing outcome ascertainment.

## Response Variable and Factors

The primary response variable is time-to-event: days from randomization to progression to an AIDS-defining illness or death, whichever occurred first. Participants who experienced neither outcome were censored at last contact. The primary factor of interest is treatment assignment (indinavir versus control). This paper additionally examines participant sex (female versus male) and race/ethnicity (White non-Hispanic, Black non-Hispanic, Hispanic, Asian/Pacific Islander, and Other) as potential effect modifiers. All models adjust for the following baseline covariates: age, CD4 cell count, Karnofsky performance score, months of prior ZDV use, and CD4 count stratum.

## Strengths and Weaknesses

The design's strengths are substantial: randomization eliminates confounding in expectation, double-blinding prevents ascertainment bias, and stratified randomization ensures balance on disease severity. The large overall enrollment provided strong power for the primary comparison, and the trial produced a landmark finding that transformed HIV treatment.

The primary weakness of this reanalysis is that the trial was not designed to support subgroup inference. The trial did not specify minimum subgroup sample sizes or event count targets for demographic groups. The result is a highly asymmetric event distribution. Female participants contribute 81 of the 96 observed events. Male participants contribute only 15, fewer than the minimum of 10-15 events per predictor typically required for stable Cox model estimation. The Asian/Pacific Islander and Other subgroups contribute 3 and 1 events, respectively, making subgroup-specific estimates for these groups entirely unreliable. Additionally, the publicly available dataset omits the trial's secondary endpoints and the American Indian/Alaska Native race category present in the original protocol, restricting this reanalysis to the primary outcome across five race/ethnicity groups.
